Japan has rejected reports claiming it agreed to accept 100,000 Bangladeshi workers every year, calling the claims circulating in local media and on social media false. 

Japan's Foreign Ministry Press Secretary Toshihiro Kitamura clarified that no such agreement was reached during the October 27 summit between Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. 

The reports had suggested that Bangladesh planned to send 100,000 workers annually to Japan to meet its labour demands. Just 28 Points Separate Kane and Mbappé as Bayern Munich Star Wins One of the Closest Ballon d'Or Races Ever

The report measures happiness through people's life evaluations and examines factors including income, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom, generosity and perceptions of corruption. Improvements in employment, healthcare, education and governance remain essential to improving people's quality of life.

त्यस्तै, लुम्बिनी, कर्णाली र सुदूरपश्चिम प्रदेशका हिमाली तथा पहाडी भूभागका केही स्थानमा पनि वर्षा र हिमपातको सम्भावना छ। विशेषगरी कोशी, मधेस र बागमती प्रदेशका एक–दुई स्थानमा भारी वर्षा तथा हिमपात हुन सक्ने महाशाखाले जनाएको छ।

आज राति पनि देशभर सामान्यतया बादल लाग्नेछ। हिमाली भूभागका थोरै स्थानमा मध्यम वर्षा र हिमपात हुन सक्नेछ भने कोशी र गण्डकी प्रदेशका पहाडी भूभागका एक–दुई स्थानमा हल्का वर्षाको सम्भावना रहेको छ।

आइतबार भने मौसममा क्रमिक सुधार आउने देखिएको छ। देशभर आंशिक बदली रहने र हिमाली तथा पहाडी भूभागका एक–दुई स्थानमा हल्का वर्षा तथा हिमपात हुन सक्ने महाशाखाको पूर्वानुमान छ।

चक्रवात ‘अर्नब’को अवशेष र पश्चिमी वायुको प्रभाव आज अपराह्नदेखि क्रमशः कमजोर हुँदै जाने महाशाखाले जनाएको छ।

विभिन्न सञ्चारमाध्यमका पत्रकारहरू पक्राउ परिरहेको घटनाबारे प्रधानमन्त्री बालेन्द्र शाहको सचिवालयले आफूलाई कुनै जानकारी नभएको दाबी गरेको छ। प्रधानमन्त्री, उनको सचिवालय र प्रधानमन्त्री तथा मन्त्रिपरिषद् कार्यालयको यस घटनामा कुनै संलग्नता नरहेको सचिवालयले स्पष्ट पारेको छ।

प्रधानमन्त्रीका प्रेस तथा अनुसन्धान विज्ञ दीपा दाहालले आज विकसित घटनाक्रमबारे प्रधानमन्त्री र उनको कार्यालयलाई कुनै जानकारी नभएको बताएकी हुन्। अनलाइनखबरसँग कुरा गर्दै उनले पत्रकार पक्राउ गर्ने घटनामा प्रधानमन्त्री तथा उनको सचिवालयको कुनै भूमिका नरहेको दाबी गरिन्।

यसैबीच प्रहरीले विभिन्न सञ्चारमाध्यमका समाचार कक्षमै प्रवेश गरेर पत्रकारहरूलाई पक्राउ गरिरहेको छ। शुक्रबार नेपाल प्रेसमा कार्यरत पत्रकार विश्वमणि सुवेदी, डीएनखबरका पत्रकार धीरज बस्नेत र मोटिभेट न्युजका पत्रकार शोभराज बराल पक्राउ परेका छन्।

त्यस्तै, नयाँ पत्रिकामा कार्यरत पत्रकार नवराज मैनालीलाई पक्राउ गर्न सादा पोसाकमा खटिएका प्रहरीहरू पत्रिकाको कार्यालयमै पुगेका छन्। उनीहरूले मैनालीलाई आफूसँगै नलगी कार्यालय नछाड्ने भन्दै समाचार कक्षमै बसेको समाचारमा उल्लेख छ।

एकपछि अर्को सञ्चारमाध्यमका पत्रकार पक्राउ परेपछि प्रेस स्वतन्त्रता र समाचारको स्रोत संरक्षणको विषयमा गम्भीर प्रश्न उठेको छ। तर, प्रधानमन्त्री सचिवालयले भने घटनाबारे कुनै जानकारी नभएको र आफ्नो संलग्नता नरहेको बताएको छ।

बंगालको खाडीमा विकसित चक्रवात ‘अर्नब’ र पश्चिमी वायुको प्रभावले नेपालका अधिकांश भूभागमा वर्षा भइरहेको छ। कोशीदेखि गण्डकी प्रदेशसम्म शुक्रबार बिहानैदेखि झरी परेको छ भने वर्षा विस्तार हुँदै सुदूरपश्चिमसम्म पुगेको छ। काठमाडौं उपत्यकामा पनि रातिदेखि पानी पर्ने र रोकिने क्रम जारी छ।

जल तथा मौसम विज्ञान विभागका अनुसार पछिल्लो १२ घण्टामा कोशी प्रदेशका केही स्थानमा भारी वर्षा मापन भएको छ। धनकुटाको लेगुवाघाटमा ५२.८ मिलिमिटर र खोटाङको कुर्लेघाटमा ४८.२ मिलिमिटर वर्षा भएको छ। मौसमविद् रोजन लामिछानेका अनुसार न्यूनचापीय प्रणाली नेपालतर्फ अझै नजिकिँदै रहेकाले साँझपछि वर्षाको क्रम थप बढ्न सक्छ। विशेषगरी कोशी र बागमती प्रदेशका हिमाली क्षेत्रमा बढी वर्षा हुने सम्भावना छ।

त्रिभुवन विश्वविद्यालयका सहप्राध्यापक डा. विनोद पोखरेलले चक्रवात ‘अर्नब’को प्रभावले करिब ५ देखि १० घण्टासम्म भारी वर्षा हुन सक्ने बताएका छन्। यद्यपि वर्षाको समय, स्थान र मात्रा परिवर्तन हुन सक्ने भएकाले उनले साँझ र रातिको समयमा सतर्क रहन तथा आधिकारिक मौसम सूचना नियमित रूपमा हेर्न आग्रह गरेका छन्।

जापानका लागि प्रस्तावित नेपाली राजदूत जिज्ञान कुमार थापाबारे निर्णय लिन संसदीय सुनुवाइ समितिको बैठक आगामी सोमबार दिउँसो ३ बजे सिंहदरबारमा बस्ने भएको छ। सुनुवाइका क्रममा उठेका प्रश्नको चित्तबुझ्दो जवाफ र जापान सरकारबाट आवश्यक विवरण प्राप्त नभएपछि समितिले यसअघि उनको नाम अनुमोदन गर्ने वा नगर्ने निर्णय स्थगित गरेको थियो।

थापाको जापानको स्थायी बसोबास अनुमतिपत्र (पीआर), परिवारको पीआर, जापानमा रहेको घर–सम्पत्ति तथा त्यहाँको सरकारी निकायसँगको सम्बन्धबारे प्रश्न उठेको थियो। थापाले आफूले जापानको पीआर त्यागिसकेको बताए पनि उनकी श्रीमतीको पीआर कायमै रहेको र उनको नाममा जापानमा घरसमेत रहेको स्वीकार गरेका थिए। यसले राजदूत नियुक्तिमा स्वार्थ बाझिन सक्ने भन्दै समितिमा उजुरीसमेत परेको थियो।

यस विषयमा स्पष्ट जानकारी माग्दै समितिले परराष्ट्र मन्त्रालयमार्फत जापान सरकारसँग विवरण मागेको छ। तर, हालसम्म जापान सरकारबाट जवाफ प्राप्त भएको छैन। समितिले परराष्ट्र मन्त्रालयको रायसमेत लिएर यही कात्तिक १९ गतेभित्र थापाबारे अन्तिम निर्णय गर्ने तयारी गरेको छ।

संविधान तथा संसदीय सुनुवाइसम्बन्धी नियमअनुसार प्रस्तावित राजदूतको नाम प्राप्त भएको ४५ दिनभित्र समितिले निर्णय गर्नुपर्ने व्यवस्था छ। कात्तिक १९ गते उक्त समयसीमा पूरा हुँदैछ। निर्धारित समयभित्र समितिले निर्णय दिन नसके थापाको नाम स्वतः अनुमोदन भएको मानिनेछ। त्यसैले सोमबारको बैठकलाई उनको राजदूत नियुक्तिको भविष्य निर्धारण गर्ने महत्वपूर्ण बैठकका रूपमा हेरिएको छ।

नेपाली क्रिकेटमा नयाँ प्रतिभाको उदय भइरहेका बेला रौतहटका १६ वर्षीय राहुल यादवले नेपाल प्रिमियर लिग (एनपिएल) मा आफ्नो क्षमता प्रभावशाली रूपमा प्रमाणित गरेका छन्। कक्षा ९ मा अध्ययनरत जनकपुर बोल्ट्सका युवा मध्यम गतिका बलर राहुलले बिहीबार काठमाडौं गोर्खाजविरुद्ध चार विकेट लिएपछि उनी चर्चामा आएका छन्।

कीर्तिपुरस्थित त्रिवि क्रिकेट मैदानमा भएको खेलमा राहुलले चार ओभर बलिङ गर्दै ३१ रन खर्चिएर चार महत्वपूर्ण विकेट लिए। उनले साम हेजलेट, स्मित पटेल, काठमाडौंका कप्तान करण केसी र मोहम्मद आदिल आलमलाई आउट गरे। उनको उत्कृष्ट बलिङका कारण काठमाडौंको ब्याटिङ दबाबमा परेको थियो। काठमाडौंले दिएको ११६ रनको लक्ष्य जनकपुरले आठ विकेट बाँकी रहँदै पूरा गर्‍यो।

राहुलका लागि यो एनपिएलको दोस्रो खेल थियो। यसअघि कर्णाली याक्सविरुद्धको डेब्यू खेलमा उनले १५ रन खर्चेर दुई विकेट लिएका थिए। पहिलो खेलमा केही नर्भस भए पनि विकेट लिन सफल भएपछि आत्मविश्वास बढेको उनले बताएका छन्।

काठमाडौंविरुद्धको खेलपछि राहुलले पहिलो खेलको अनुभवले दोस्रो खेलमा राम्रो प्रदर्शन गर्न सहयोग गरेको बताए। “कर्णालीविरुद्धको पहिलो खेल एनपिएलमा मेरो पहिलो थियो। केही नर्भस थिएँ। पहिलो खेलमा विकेट लिन सफल भएपछि आज त्यो डर भाग्यो। त्यसैले आज विकेट लिन सफल भएँ,” उनले भने।

मधेश प्रदेशको रौतहटस्थित चन्द्रपुरका राहुलको क्रिकेट यात्रा खुला मैदानबाट सुरु भएको हो। चन्द्रपुर क्रिकेट एकेडेमीमा आफ्नो बलिङ कौशल निखारेका उनले कम उमेरमै बलिङको गति र क्षमताका कारण ध्यान आकर्षित गर्न थालेका थिए। उनका बुबाले क्रिकेट नबुझे पनि आफूलाई निरन्तर साथ र समर्थन दिँदै आएको राहुलले बताएका छन्।

जनकपुर बोल्ट्सले आयोजना गरेको ट्यालेन्ट हन्टबाट छनोट भएपछि उनी टोलीमा आइकोनिक खेलाडीका रूपमा आबद्ध भएका हुन्। स्थानीय स्तरबाट प्रतिभा पहिचान गर्ने प्रतियोगितामार्फत राष्ट्रिय स्तरको फ्रेन्चाइज लिगसम्म पुग्नु राहुलको क्रिकेट यात्राको महत्वपूर्ण उपलब्धि बनेको छ।

एनपिएलअघि चन्द्रपुर क्रिकेट लिगमा पनि उनले राम्रो प्रदर्शन गरेका थिए। उक्त प्रतियोगितामा म्यान अफ द म्याच बनेका राहुलले एनपिएलमा समेत आफ्नो क्षमता देखाउने संकेत गरेका थिए। कर्णालीविरुद्ध दुई विकेट र त्यसपछि काठमाडौंविरुद्ध चार विकेट लिनुले उनको आत्मविश्वास र सम्भावनालाई थप उजागर गरेको छ।

कक्षा ९ को पढाइसँगै नेपाली क्रिकेटको ठूलो मञ्चमा आफ्नो प्रतिभा देखाइरहेका राहुलको प्रदर्शनले नयाँ पुस्ताका खेलाडीप्रति आशा जगाएको छ। १६ वर्षकै उमेरमा एनपिएलमा प्रभाव छाड्न सफल उनको यो सुरुवात आगामी क्रिकेट यात्राका लागि उत्साहजनक संकेत बनेको छ।

स्पेनको मध्य क्षेत्रमा भएको भीषण रेल दुर्घटनाले ६९ जनाको ज्यान लिएको छ। सयभन्दा बढी यात्रु घाइते भएका छन्। तर यो दुर्घटनाले ज्यान गुमाउनेमध्ये २४ वर्षीया युवा एथलेटिक्स खेलाडी जुलिएटा गालेगोको निधनले खेलकुद जगत्‌लाई विशेष रूपमा स्तब्ध बनाएको छ।

सानै उमेरमा खेलकुदमा आफ्नो पहिचान बनाउँदै भविष्यका लागि सपना सजाइरहेकी जुलिएटाको जीवनयात्रा रेल दुर्घटनासँगै अचानक समाप्त भएको छ। उनी म्याड्रिडस्थित एथलेटिक्स क्लब एडी स्प्रिन्टबाट लङ जम्प प्रतियोगितामा सहभागी हुँदै आएकी थिइन्। उनले आफ्नो उत्कृष्ट प्रदर्शनमा ५.९ मिटरको छलाङ लगाएकी थिइन्। तर अब उनको खेल मैदानमा फर्किने सपना कहिल्यै पूरा हुने छैन।

स्पेनको रोयल एथलेटिक्स महासंघले जुलिएटाको निधनप्रति गहिरो दुःख व्यक्त गर्दै उनलाई श्रद्धाञ्जली दिएको छ। महासंघले उनको निधनलाई एथलेटिक्स समुदायका लागि अपूरणीय क्षति भनेको छ। २४ वर्षको उमेरमै सम्भावनाले भरिएको जीवन गुमाउनु उनका परिवार, साथीभाइ र खेलकुद क्षेत्रका लागि असह्य पीडा बनेको छ।

बुधबार बिहान मध्य स्पेनको उर्दा नजिकै तीव्र गतिमा गुडिरहेको रेन्फे रेल र रोकिराखिएको इरियो रेल एउटै ट्र्याकमा ठोक्किएका थिए। भीषण ठक्करपछि रेलका कैयौँ डिब्बा लिकबाट बाहिरिएका थिए। दुर्घटनामा ६९ जनाको मृत्यु भएको छ भने सयभन्दा बढी घाइते भएका छन्। घाइतेमध्ये धेरैको अवस्था गम्भीर रहेको बताइएको छ। मृतकको संख्या अझै बढ्न सक्ने अधिकारीहरूले आशंका गरेका छन्।

प्रहरीको अनुसन्धान अब मुख्यतः दुई प्रश्नमा केन्द्रित छ। पहिलो, दुर्घटनामा मृत्यु भएका व्यक्तिको वास्तविक पहिचान के थियो? दोस्रो, परिवारले उक्त शवलाई पदमबहादुरकै शव भनेर कसरी सनाखत गर्‍यो?

प्रहरीका अनुसार घटना सुनसरीको बराहक्षेत्र नगरपालिका–४ स्थित चतरा–पकली सडकखण्डमा भएको थियो। २०८३ जेठ २६ गते बिहान करिब साढे ८ बजे मोटरसाइकलको ठक्करबाट एक पैदलयात्री गम्भीर घाइते भएका थिए।

उपचारका लागि उनलाई बुढीगंगास्थित विराट टिचिङ अस्पताल लगिएको थियो। उपचारकै क्रममा मृत्यु भएपछि शव कोशी अस्पतालको शवगृहमा राखिएको थियो। मृतकको पहिचान खुल्न नसकेपछि प्रहरीले आफन्तलाई सम्पर्कमा आउन सार्वजनिक सूचना जारी गरेको थियो।

प्रहरीको सूचनापछि पदमबहादुरकी आमा अस्पताल पुगेकी थिइन्। उनले शव आफ्नै छोराको भएको बताएपछि प्रहरीले आवश्यक प्रक्रिया पूरा गरी शव परिवारलाई बुझाएको थियो। परिवारले त्यसपछि अन्त्येष्टि गरेको थियो।

लामो समय घरबाहिर थिए पदमबहादुर
इलाका प्रहरी कार्यालय लेटाङका अनुसार पदमबहादुर २०८२ माघदेखि घरबाहिर थिए। उनी घर छाडेर हिँड्ने गरेको जानकारी प्रहरीले परिवारबाट पाएको छ।

विवाहपछि श्रीमती अलग्गिएसँगै पदमबहादुर घरमा नियमित रूपमा नबस्ने गरेको बताइएको छ। लामो समय घरबाहिर रहेकाले परिवारलाई उनको अवस्थाबारे जानकारी थिएन।

यही परिस्थितिमा दुर्घटनामा मृत्यु भएका अज्ञात व्यक्तिको शव देखेपछि आमाले आफ्नै छोराको ठानेर सनाखत गरेको हुन सक्ने प्रहरीको प्रारम्भिक बुझाइ छ। तर, त्यसबेला शवको पहिचान कसरी गलत भयो भन्ने विषयमा अनुसन्धानबाट थप तथ्य खुल्न बाँकी छ।

बीमा रकम पनि अनुसन्धानको दायरामा
पदमबहादुर जीवितै फर्किएपछि परिवारले प्राप्त गरेको ५ लाख ५० हजार रुपैयाँको दुर्घटना बीमाबारे पनि प्रश्न उठेको छ। प्रहरीका अनुसार परिवारले उक्त रकम फिर्ता गर्ने बताएको छ।

अब प्रहरीले दुर्घटनामा मृत्यु भएका व्यक्तिको वास्तविक पहिचान पत्ता लगाउने, शव सनाखत प्रक्रियाको पुनः परीक्षण गर्ने र घटनासँग सम्बन्धित विवरण स्पष्ट पार्ने काम अघि बढाउनेछ।

पदमबहादुर जीवितै घर फर्किए पनि उनको मृत्यु भएको ठानेर अन्त्येष्टि गरिएको व्यक्तिको पहिचान अझै खुल्न सकेको छैन। प्रहरीको अनुसन्धानपछि मात्रै घटनाको वास्तविकता स्पष्ट हुनेछ।

A WWII DESTROYER WAS FOUND MORE THAN 6,400 METRES UNDER THE OCEAN!

For decades, the USS Johnston rested in the darkness of the Philippine Sea, more than 6 kilometres beneath the surface.

The American destroyer sank on October 25, 1944, during the Battle off Samar in World War II. Despite facing a vastly larger Japanese force, the ship fought to protect vulnerable American escort carriers.

In 2019, explorers located wreckage believed to be the Johnston. But the mystery was finally solved in March 2021, when a crewed deep-sea submersible reached the main wreck at approximately 6,456 metres (21,180 feet).

The biggest confirmation?

The ship’s hull number 557 was still visible after more than 76 years underwater.

Of the 327 crew members, 141 survived.

Imagine discovering a ship resting in complete darkness, with its identity still written on its bow after all those years.

“WE WERE STACKING SO MANY BODIES THAT PATROLS HAD TO GO OUT TO MOVE THEM OFF OUR FIELDS OF FIRE.” — Marine Raider Cody Alford on the Battle of Fallujah on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most intense firsthand accounts of modern urban warfare ever recorded on The Shawn Ryan Show, former Marine Raider and Scout Sniper Cody Alford broke down the brutal house-to-house meatgrinder of Operation Phantom Fury—and the terrifying out-of-body experience he suffered after taking an insurgent sniper bullet directly to the helmet.

In his own words:

“The night prior to going in, my platoon commander walks in and says, ‘Everyone is going to write their death letter.’

I’m 18 years old, sitting there thinking: What do you even write? I wrote a letter to my girlfriend, wrote one to my parents, turned them over to the platoon commander, and that’s when I knew shit was real.

In Fallujah, the brutality of what we were up against was beyond comprehension. The human shields, the mutilations, the sheer volume of combat. We were stacking so many bodies that we had to send patrols out into the street just to drag bodies out of the way because they were blocking our fields of fire.

I remember stepping behind a window frame, slamming in a fresh magazine, and as soon as I pop out to shoot, everything goes black.

A profound exhale left my body, and I hit the deck. That’s when I had this out-of-body experience. It was like a video game glitch—a top-down view looking down at the entire scene. I could see the fighters across the street. I could see my own body lying still. I could see my point man still firing. I saw this blinding light, thinking: I’m f**king dead.

Then suddenly, I got sucked back into my body. I came to curled up in a fetal position with my buddy kicking my leg shouting, ‘Wake up! We thought you were dead!’

The bullet had hit me flush in the helmet.”

The Second Battle of Fallujah stands as the bloodiest, most relentless urban combat the U.S. Marine Corps has fought since the Battle of Huế City in 1968.

Something quietly significant is happening in the world's weapons factories. The United States and Japan have agreed to start building advanced missiles together, in Japan, driven by two pressures pulling the same way: American stockpiles are running low after years of conflict, and China is expanding its own arsenal fast.

The deal, reached by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Japan's Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, has two parts: a new factory in Japan to build AMRAAM air-to-air missiles, and a push to ramp up production of the SM-3, a ship-launched interceptor. It falls under a program the allies call Operation Supercharge.

The urgency is real. Years of arming Ukraine and the recent campaign against Iran drew down US munitions, and in May the Pentagon listed both these missiles among 14 it wants built faster. Meanwhile, a CNN analysis last year found expansion at more than 60% of 136 Chinese missile-production sites.

It's a statement of intent for now, with quantities and timelines still unannounced, and factories take years. But the lesson underneath is clear: in a long war, what matters may be less who has the best weapon than who can keep making them.

Footage recorded outside the ICE processing facility in Broadview, Illinois, has triggered a nationwide debate over lawful protest, federal authority, and the boundaries of reasonable force.

In the viral clip, an activist holding an umbrella stands squarely in front of an official ICE SUV, refusing repeated directives to clear the driveway during an active enforcement operation. A federal agent in tactical gear steps up, shoves her aside to clear the vehicle’s path, and she falls onto the wet asphalt before agents proceed.

Critics and civil rights activists were quick to label the shove police brutality, citing 18 U.S.C. § 242 (deprivation of rights under color of law) and arguing the force used was unnecessary against a non-violent demonstrator.

Federal law enforcement advocates and legal analysts counter that intentional physical obstruction of official government vehicles constitutes interference under 18 U.S.C. § 111. Under established federal standards, officers are legally authorized to apply proportional, minimal physical force to remove active barricades and hazards from transit paths so lawful operations can continue safely.

Public reactions from viewers who analyzed the unedited footage:

“The right to protest doesn’t include blocking traffic, breaking laws, and obstructing federal vehicles.”

“That was measured, reasonable force to clear an active obstruction. When someone repeatedly refuses lawful orders to step aside, officers have an obligation to clear the roadway.”

“Protest rights protect speech, but they do not provide a license to physically impede law enforcement operations.”

Federal agents have a statutory duty to carry out operations directed by Congress. While peaceful assembly remains constitutionally protected, physically blocking official vehicles escalates a demonstration into an active obstruction hazard.

Where do you draw the line? Was the officer’s action a lawful, necessary clearance to maintain operations, or did it cross into excessive force?

“DON’T WASTE YOUR TIME ON ME. I AM IN THE EXPECTANT CATEGORY. I’M DONE HERE.” — Green Beret Warrant Officer Nick Lavery on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most unforgettable moments on The Shawn Ryan Show, Special Forces Warrant Officer Nick "The Machine" Lavery recounted the insider attack in Afghanistan where he threw himself in front of a rookie soldier to absorb point-blank machine gun fire.

In his own words:

“I snap my head around and see what’s happening. A gunner 15 feet away from the group ripping into the crowd with a PKM. Guys are dropping. Chaos.

My training tells me: move to cover, eliminate the threat. But six feet in front of me is one of our infantry uplift soldiers—young kid, first deployment, fresh out of basic. He’s 15 feet in front of a guy shooting a machine gun in his general direction, frozen like a deer in the headlights.

Seeing that prompted me to move towards him rather than to cover. I put myself in between him and the shooter, back to the gun. I hit him with such velocity that when we made contact, I took a round to the back of my leg.

I fall chest to chest on top of him. A PKM from 15 feet feels like a sledgehammer smashing into your body. Then boom, boom, boom a couple more impacts.

I check the kid. He’s in shock, pale, but no holes in his body. He’s breathing.

So now let’s see what’s going on with me. I rip open what’s left of my pant leg. My right leg is just f**king mangled—hanging meat, tissue, and exposed bone. I am hissing blood out of my thigh. There is a river flowing from where I was struck. My femoral artery is severed. I have maybe eight or nine minutes before I bleed out completely.

Imagine being strapped into a seat facing backward, in the windowless belly of a propeller plane on the deck of an aircraft carrier in the middle of the ocean. A catapult grabs the plane, and in about two seconds you go from a dead stop to roughly 130 miles an hour and off the bow, slammed back into your seat the whole way.

For 60 years, this was the normal way to reach a US Navy carrier at sea, and the plane that did it was the C-2 Greyhound. The landing was just as wild: the Greyhound caught a steel cable with a hook on its tail, going from flying speed to a dead stop in under 400 feet. First-timers never forgot it.

But it was far more than a thrill ride. Its job was Carrier Onboard Delivery, flying the parts, people, and mail a carrier needs out to the ship while it is underway, sometimes hundreds of miles from land. And of everything it carried, nothing meant more to the crews than the mail: the letters and packages from home that a sailor on a long deployment waits weeks to hold. A single pair of Greyhounds could move a million pounds of cargo and 5,000 passengers in one deployment. Quietly, it kept the world's most powerful warships running.

After six decades, the Greyhound flew its last flight earlier in 2026, retired to a museum in Pensacola and replaced by the CMV-22B Osprey. "It's very sad to me," said the pilot of that final flight, "but I feel a lot of satisfaction that we did it safely."

How much has the war with Iran cost the United States? It is a simple question with a surprisingly slippery answer.

That is a big reason the estimates vary so much: an earlier public figure put the cost around 25 billion, while US officials told CBS and CNN the real total was already closer to 40 to 50 billion, and some projections run higher still once long-term costs like replacing munitions are counted.

None of the numbers is exactly wrong. They are measuring different things over different timeframes. The honest answer to what the Iran war has cost is a range, not a single figure: at least 47 billion by the military's own count, and quite possibly more once the full picture comes in.

Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. For the first time since the Korean War, the U.S. Army is actively preparing for the grimmest reality of large-scale combat: digging temporary mass graves directly on the battlefield.

During recent high-intensity readiness exercises at Fort Liberty, North Carolina, combat engineers from the 20th Engineer Brigade, soldiers from the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, mortuary affairs specialists, and Army chaplains trained with heavy bulldozers and excavators to establish standardized field burial sites.

The metrics from the exercise are chilling:

Standardized burial trenches for 20 fallen soldiers can be excavated in just 75 minutes.

Using eight bulldozers and four military excavators, an engineering unit could temporarily inter the remains of up to 2,400 soldiers within a single 24-hour window.

For the past 20 years in Iraq and Afghanistan, the U.S. military enjoyed complete air dominance. Every fallen warrior was treated with reverent custody and flown directly home to Dover Air Force Base within days.

But Pentagon war games for a potential clash against a near-peer adversary—such as China or Russia—reveal a brutal reality:

Contested airspace, anti-ship missiles, and cyber-disrupted logistics could sever supply lines for weeks.

Immediate air repatriation would be physically impossible, and casualty counts could reach thousands in days.

Frontline units would be forced to temporarily inter fallen soldiers in the dirt to maintain positive identification, prevent disease, and protect remains until the combat zone can be secured for repatriation.

As Sergeant 1st Class Delbert Ruede stated during the drills: "If we went to war tomorrow, we would be making this up as we went along. What we are doing here is taking a scientific, field-tested approach so that we can maintain positive control and respectfully care for our fallen."

Practicing the unthinkable is the starkest sign yet of how seriously military planners view the threat of major war.

Is the military being responsibly realistic about near-peer warfare, or is this a chilling warning of where global tensions are heading?

March 4, 2002. A 10,000-foot freezing mountain peak in eastern Afghanistan: Takur Ghar.

When a Navy SEAL was thrown from a damaged Chinook into an enemy hornets' nest, Air Force Combat Controller John Chapman volunteered to go back onto that mountain to get his brother back.

As soon as their helicopter touched down, they were hit with RPGs and heavy machine-gun fire. Chapman charged uphill alone through thigh-deep snow, assaulted an al-Qaeda bunker, and neutralized the fighters inside.

While assaulting a second bunker, he was shot multiple times and knocked unconscious. Believed to be fallen, his team was forced to break contact down the mountain.

But John Chapman wasn’t dead.

Sixteen years later, declassified high-definition drone footage revealed the truth: Chapman woke up alone on that freezing peak. Severely wounded and surrounded by dozens of enemy fighters, he refused to quit.

For over an hour, he fought a solo one-man stand from a snow bunker.

When an inbound quick-reaction helicopter carrying 18 Army Rangers flew directly into the ambush zone, Chapman knew they would be shredded.

He made his final choice: he stepped out of his bunker into the open, drawing all enemy fire toward himself to protect the landing helicopter until he was mortally wounded.

His solo stand saved the lives of every man on that incoming bird.

In 2018, Master Sergeant John Chapman was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor—the first Air Force special operator to receive it since Vietnam.

On February 1, 1943, a B-17 Flying Fortress named the All American did something a plane simply isn't supposed to survive: it was cut nearly in half in mid-air, and flew home anyway.

Coming off a raid on the German-held Tunisian coast, the All American was struck when a German Messerschmitt fighter, diving in to attack, failed to pull up in time and slammed into its tail at full speed. The collision sheared through the fuselage and nearly cut the plane in two, just behind the radio compartment. The entire tail section was left hanging on by a few thin metal strips, twisting in the wind as if it might snap off at any second. By every rule of physics, the plane should have broken apart. It didn't.

The pilot, Lt. Kendrick Bragg, nursed the shattered aircraft home with the gentlest possible touch, the crew using parachute harnesses and debris to help hold the tail on. Not one man aboard had been killed or even seriously hurt. They chose to fly it home rather than bail out, limped back across North Africa, and landed. Every single man walked away alive. It remains one of the greatest testaments ever to the toughness of the B-17, the plane that brought its crews home.

“WE WERE STACKING SO MANY BODIES THAT PATROLS HAD TO GO OUT TO MOVE THEM OFF OUR FIELDS OF FIRE.” — Marine Raider Cody Alford on the Battle of Fallujah on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most intense firsthand accounts of modern urban warfare ever recorded on The Shawn Ryan Show, former Marine Raider and Scout Sniper Cody Alford broke down the brutal house-to-house meatgrinder of Operation Phantom Fury—and the terrifying out-of-body experience he suffered after taking an insurgent sniper bullet directly to the helmet.

In his own words:

“The night prior to going in, my platoon commander walks in and says, ‘Everyone is going to write their death letter.’

I’m 18 years old, sitting there thinking: What do you even write? I wrote a letter to my girlfriend, wrote one to my parents, turned them over to the platoon commander, and that’s when I knew shit was real.

In Fallujah, the brutality of what we were up against was beyond comprehension. The human shields, the mutilations, the sheer volume of combat. We were stacking so many bodies that we had to send patrols out into the street just to drag bodies out of the way because they were blocking our fields of fire.

I remember stepping behind a window frame, slamming in a fresh magazine, and as soon as I pop out to shoot, everything goes black.

A profound exhale left my body, and I hit the deck. That’s when I had this out-of-body experience. It was like a video game glitch—a top-down view looking down at the entire scene. I could see the fighters across the street. I could see my own body lying still. I could see my point man still firing. I saw this blinding light, thinking: I’m f**king dead.

Then suddenly, I got sucked back into my body. I came to curled up in a fetal position with my buddy kicking my leg shouting, ‘Wake up! We thought you were dead!’

The bullet had hit me flush in the helmet.”

The Second Battle of Fallujah stands as the bloodiest, most relentless urban combat the U.S. Marine Corps has fought since the Battle of Huế City in 1968.

“DON’T WASTE YOUR TIME ON ME. I AM IN THE EXPECTANT CATEGORY. I’M DONE HERE.” — Green Beret Warrant Officer Nick Lavery on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most unforgettable moments on The Shawn Ryan Show, Special Forces Warrant Officer Nick "The Machine" Lavery recounted the insider attack in Afghanistan where he threw himself in front of a rookie soldier to absorb point-blank machine gun fire.

In his own words:

“I snap my head around and see what’s happening. A gunner 15 feet away from the group ripping into the crowd with a PKM. Guys are dropping. Chaos.

My training tells me: move to cover, eliminate the threat. But six feet in front of me is one of our infantry uplift soldiers—young kid, first deployment, fresh out of basic. He’s 15 feet in front of a guy shooting a machine gun in his general direction, frozen like a deer in the headlights.

Seeing that prompted me to move towards him rather than to cover. I put myself in between him and the shooter, back to the gun. I hit him with such velocity that when we made contact, I took a round to the back of my leg.

I fall chest to chest on top of him. A PKM from 15 feet feels like a sledgehammer smashing into your body. Then boom, boom, boom a couple more impacts.

I check the kid. He’s in shock, pale, but no holes in his body. He’s breathing.

So now let’s see what’s going on with me. I rip open what’s left of my pant leg. My right leg is just f**king mangled—hanging meat, tissue, and exposed bone. I am hissing blood out of my thigh. There is a river flowing from where I was struck. My femoral artery is severed. I have maybe eight or nine minutes before I bleed out completely.

One of my teammates gets over to me. The look on his face said everything: Nick’s not going to make it.

I looked at him and said, ‘Listen man, go work on someone you can save. I am in the expectant category here in triage. Don’t waste your time, precious seconds, and resources on me, because I’m done here.’”

His teammates refused to quit on him. They cranked tourniquets onto his mangled leg, stabilized him under fire, and got him on a medevac bird.

Not only did Nick survive having his leg amputated above the knee, but he also refused medical retirement. He underwent grueling rehab, relearned how to shoot, sprint, and clear rooms on a carbon-fiber prosthetic, and became the first active-duty Green Beret in history to return to combat as an above-the-knee amputee.

Ordering your brothers to leave you behind to save others while you bleed out from a severed femoral artery is the ultimate definition of selfless service.

For the first time since the Korean War, the U.S. Army is actively preparing for the grimmest reality of large-scale combat: digging temporary mass graves directly on the battlefield.

During recent high-intensity readiness exercises at Fort Liberty, North Carolina, combat engineers from the 20th Engineer Brigade, soldiers from the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, mortuary affairs specialists, and Army chaplains trained with heavy bulldozers and excavators to establish standardized field burial sites.

The metrics from the exercise are chilling:

Standardized burial trenches for 20 fallen soldiers can be excavated in just 75 minutes.

Using eight bulldozers and four military excavators, an engineering unit could temporarily inter the remains of up to 2,400 soldiers within a single 24-hour window.

For the past 20 years in Iraq and Afghanistan, the U.S. military enjoyed complete air dominance. Every fallen warrior was treated with reverent custody and flown directly home to Dover Air Force Base within days.

But Pentagon war games for a potential clash against a near-peer adversary—such as China or Russia—reveal a brutal reality:

Contested airspace, anti-ship missiles, and cyber-disrupted logistics could sever supply lines for weeks.

Frontline units would be forced to temporarily inter fallen soldiers in the dirt to maintain positive identification, prevent disease, and protect remains until the combat zone can be secured for repatriation.

Practicing the unthinkable is the starkest sign yet of how seriously military planners view the threat of major war.

The sudden temperature overrides thawed massive freezer rows, spoiling hundreds of thousands of dollars in groceries and leaving military families with empty shelves.

Federal investigators quickly connected the dots: the incident closely mirrors a sophisticated cyberattack in France that remotely hacked and shut down environmental cooling controls across more than 350 commercial supermarkets.

While spoiled commissary food might sound like an annoyance on the surface, cybersecurity and military intelligence analysts warn that this is a classic asymmetric infrastructure probe:

Operational Technology (OT) Infiltration: Hostile nation-state hacking groups (such as China or Russia) are actively testing their ability to breach the industrial control systems and software running U.S. military installations.

The Wartime Threat: If foreign hackers can remotely shut down cooling systems in base grocery stores, the exact same networked SCADA vulnerabilities can be used during a conflict to overheat classified supercomputer data centers, ruin temperature-sensitive missile propellant in munitions depots, and destroy military medical blood and vaccine banks.

Gray-zone cyber warfare isn't coming in the future—it's already hitting domestic bases inside our own borders.

Is targeting grocery stores and base infrastructure an early warning of a massive cyber conflict, or are military networks too vulnerable to basic commercial hacking?

March 4, 2002. A 10,000-foot freezing mountain peak in eastern Afghanistan: Takur Ghar.

When a Navy SEAL was thrown from a damaged Chinook into an enemy hornets' nest, Air Force Combat Controller John Chapman volunteered to go back onto that mountain to get his brother back.

As soon as their helicopter touched down, they were hit with RPGs and heavy machine-gun fire. Chapman charged uphill alone through thigh-deep snow, assaulted an al-Qaeda bunker, and neutralized the fighters inside.

While assaulting a second bunker, he was shot multiple times and knocked unconscious. Believed to be fallen, his team was forced to break contact down the mountain.

But John Chapman wasn’t dead.

Sixteen years later, declassified high-definition drone footage revealed the truth: Chapman woke up alone on that freezing peak. Severely wounded and surrounded by dozens of enemy fighters, he refused to quit.

For over an hour, he fought a solo one-man stand from a snow bunker.

When an inbound quick-reaction helicopter carrying 18 Army Rangers flew directly into the ambush zone, Chapman knew they would be shredded.

He made his final choice: he stepped out of his bunker into the open, drawing all enemy fire toward himself to protect the landing helicopter until he was mortally wounded.

His solo stand saved the lives of every man on that incoming bird.

In 2018, Master Sergeant John Chapman was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor—the first Air Force special operator to receive it since Vietnam.

“WE WERE STACKING SO MANY BODIES THAT PATROLS HAD TO GO OUT TO MOVE THEM OFF OUR FIELDS OF FIRE.” — Marine Raider Cody Alford on the Battle of Fallujah on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most intense firsthand accounts of modern urban warfare ever recorded on The Shawn Ryan Show, former Marine Raider and Scout Sniper Cody Alford broke down the brutal house-to-house meatgrinder of Operation Phantom Fury—and the terrifying out-of-body experience he suffered after taking an insurgent sniper bullet directly to the helmet.

In his own words:

“The night prior to going in, my platoon commander walks in and says, ‘Everyone is going to write their death letter.’

I’m 18 years old, sitting there thinking: What do you even write? I wrote a letter to my girlfriend, wrote one to my parents, turned them over to the platoon commander, and that’s when I knew shit was real.

In Fallujah, the brutality of what we were up against was beyond comprehension. The human shields, the mutilations, the sheer volume of combat. We were stacking so many bodies that we had to send patrols out into the street just to drag bodies out of the way because they were blocking our fields of fire.

I remember stepping behind a window frame, slamming in a fresh magazine, and as soon as I pop out to shoot, everything goes black.

A profound exhale left my body, and I hit the deck. That’s when I had this out-of-body experience. It was like a video game glitch—a top-down view looking down at the entire scene. I could see the fighters across the street. I could see my own body lying still. I could see my point man still firing. I saw this blinding light, thinking: I’m f**king dead.

Then suddenly, I got sucked back into my body. I came to curled up in a fetal position with my buddy kicking my leg shouting, ‘Wake up! We thought you were dead!’

The bullet had hit me flush in the helmet.”

The Second Battle of Fallujah stands as the bloodiest, most relentless urban combat the U.S. Marine Corps has fought since the Battle of Huế City in 1968.

Citation of Distinguished Service Cross, posthumous

CW4 Keith Yoakum,
Alpha Company, 1st Battalion, 227th Aviation Regiment
1st Air Cavalry Brigade, Multi-National Division (Baghdad)

CW4 Keith Yoakum distinguished himself by gallantry and courage at the risk of his own life above and beyond the call of duty as an AH-64D Longbow Apache Pilot-in Command while providing cover for his wingman on 2 February 2007 during aerial combat against a deliberate helicopter ambush site.

The previous two weeks in the Baghdad area of operations witnessed four separate attacks on coalition aircraft, resulting in the loss of 19 lives and the destruction of one AH-64D Longbow Apache, one UH-60 Blackhawk, and two Department of Defense contracted helicopters. CW4 Yoakum was the first responder to the UH-60 crash site and was intimately familiar with the enemy's helicopter ambush tactics.

CW4 Yoakum was the Pilot-in-Command of the trail aircraft in a flight of two AH-64D Longbow Apache helicopters as they departed on a reconnaissance mission in support of four separate ground brigades on the morning of 2 February 2007. Just when the Apache team began reconnaissance of a test fire area, waves of red tracers and heavy machine gun fire burst into the sky from multiple directions and raked the Apaches. The tracer fire immediately engulfed CW4 Yoakum's aircraft and riddled his fuselage. The enemy had established a deadly kill zone comprised of multiple heavy machine gun and anti-aircraft gun positions. With its interlocking fields of heavy anti-aircraft fire, the enemy ambush site was similar to the earlier ambush site that had downed a UH-60—the same UH-60 that CW4 Yoakum had responded to 13 days earlier, thus familiarizing him with the lethality of the enemy's tactics.

CW4 Yoakum immediately radioed his lead aircraft to maneuver it away from the direction of fire. As the lead aircraft broke hard to the right, the enemy responded, shifting its fire away from CW4 Yoakum's aircraft and toward the lead aircraft. CW4 Yoakum warned the lead helicopter announcing “now you're taking fire!” and the two aircraft broke left to escape the deadly kill zone.

Despite the damage to his aircraft, CW4 Yoakum took personal charge of the team amid the melee of bullets, calmed his lead aircraft, and steered the team out of the kill zone. The team raced to the north to separate from the enemy force and to acquire standoff range to assess the situation. Immediately after their turn to the north, CW4 Yoakum announced that he had “lost utility hydraulics,” a condition that requires the pilot to land the aircraft immediately at the nearest clear landing area. As the senior maintenance test pilot in the company, a prior instructor to other maintenance test pilots, and a Master Army Aviator with almost 5000 flight hours, CW4 Yoakum instantly understood the gravity of his Apache's emergency condition. Furthermore, CW4 Yoakum recognized that the loss of hydraulic pressure prevented him from employing his aircraft's main gun. As a result, he would have to use the aircraft's 2.75 inch rockets from a fixed position, requiring him to skillfully maneuver his crippled aircraft to accurately employ the rockets against the enemy.

The team continued northbound and after approximately two minutes no longer had tracers whipping by their windscreens. Once clear of the immediate threat, CW4 Yoakum had the opportunity to fly his critically damaged aircraft back to the airfield or land in the open desert to conduct an emergency extraction of his crew on his wingman's aircraft. He again announced “we've got no utility hydraulics left.” Still, despite the cockpit warnings and CW4 Yoakum's own recognition of his grave situation, he never considered leaving his wingman and knew this enemy would kill again if left on the battlefield. The enemy had a distinct advantage as a result of their concealed position among the numerous canals and irrigation ditches in the surrounding countryside. Despite the fierce danger inherent in pressing the attack, CW4 Yoakum radioed his wingman that “I can put rockets in” and continued to plan the route back into the withering fire of the enemy's ambush site to destroy the enemy's anti-aircraft positions.

CW4 Yoakum's instructions to his lead aircraft were simple: “you find them, we've got you covered.” CW4 Yoakum knew that his Apache team had a sliver of an opportunity to engage and destroy the enemy before they blended into the Iraqi countryside. The team decided to search the ambush area in a cloverleaf pattern, thereby performing a sweep of the area from all directions until they were able to locate the anti-aircraft guns. Despite his aircraft's crippled condition and the knowledge of the volume of fire that would again rake his aircraft at the ambush site, CW4 Yoakum was determined to cover his wingman as they searched for targets and eliminated the enemy position which was certain to be set up again at a different time and place to destroy coalition aircraft.

Approximately two minutes after the initial ambush had crippled CW4 Yoakum's Apache, the lead aircraft, acting on CW4 Yoakum's instructions, turned south to begin their search for the enemy ambush site. Despite the deteriorating condition of his own aircraft, CW4 Yoakum announced “I'm going to climb up and cover you from high and we're gonna work on rockets.” As he continued losing critical hydraulic pressure, CW4 Yoakum determined that his degraded weapons systems necessitated that he climb to altitude and then dive his damaged aircraft directly at the enemy to provide effective rocket fire. Only by diving from a higher altitude directly toward the enemy position could he provide precise rocket fire for his wingman while focusing his fires solely on the enemy and away from the surrounding villages and homes in the Iraqi countryside. With unmatched skill and extraordinary courage, CW4 Yoakum began his climb to posture his crippled aircraft in a diving position, knowing full well that his climb would give the enemy gunners a clearer line of sight and more time with which to engage his aircraft as he maneuvered back towards the ambush site.

CW4 Yoakum's focus on the destruction of the enemy's anti-aircraft guns caused him to demand as much from his aircraft as he did from himself, but his dying Apache was not able to sustain its altitude. As the Apache team made a second inbound run to the ambush area utilizing their cloverleaf pattern, the lead Apache radioed to CW4 Yoakum to ensure that he was still with them. After transmitting several radio calls and receiving no response, the lead aircraft began a left turn and acquired CW4 Yoakum's aircraft. After flying for almost four minutes in a critical state, CW4 Yoakum's Apache had succumbed to its battle damage and was engulfed in a blazing fire on the ground following a crash that had instantly killed CW4 Yoakum and his copilot.

CW4 Yoakum acted to protect his wingman and destroy an enemy anti-aircraft position designed to produce the continued loss of coalition aircraft. His decision to knowingly risk his life to cover his lead aircraft, despite having the opportunity to land or return to the airfield, put the accomplishment of his mission and the protection of his comrades over his own personal safety. His personal bravery and uncommon valor at the risk of his own life reflects great credit upon himself, the 1st Air Cavalry Brigade, the First Cavalry Division and the Multinational Division-Baghdad, and the United States Army.

On April 7, 2003, during the fierce opening days of Operation Iraqi Freedom, U.S. Air Force Captain (later Colonel) Kim "Killer Chick" Campbell cemented her place in aviation legend when her A-10 Thunderbolt II took a direct hit over downtown Baghdad—and she refused to bail out.   

While diving below cloud cover to deliver close-air support for pinned-down U.S. ground troops near the Tigris River, Campbell had just finished firing her 30mm GAU-8 Avenger cannon and rockets when a surface-to-air missile slammed into the rear of her Warthog. The blast shredded her horizontal stabilizer, punched over 150 shrapnel holes into the fuselage and right engine cowling, and instantly severed both redundant hydraulic systems. 

As the crippled jet rolled violently left and pitched straight toward the streets of central Baghdad, Campbell knew ejecting meant parachuting directly into enemy hands. In a split second, she flipped the switch to manual reversion—a mechanical backup system of pulleys, cranks, and steel cables that pilots compare to steering a heavy truck with the stick stuck in quick-setting cement. 

Escorted by her flight lead, Lt. Col. Richard "Bino" Turner, Campbell muscled the battered Warthog for an hour over 300 miles back to Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait. Rather than ejecting over friendly territory as the flight manual suggests, she elected to land the aircraft with no hydraulic flight controls, no speed brakes, and no normal steering—setting it down so smoothly that the wing's chief of safety remarked she landed it better with no hydraulics than most pilots do with all systems operational. She was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for her extraordinary airmanship under fire.

A comprehensive U.S. Army medical study examining the brutal physical toll of Ranger School has revealed that female soldiers who complete the course finish in better overall physiological condition than their male counterparts, experiencing significantly less hormonal disruption and preserving a higher percentage of lean muscle mass.

While male soldiers entered and exited the course with higher absolute strength and power, their bodies experienced a far steeper physiological crash. Men lost significantly more total body mass and lean muscle tissue, whereas female candidates metabolized fat stores more efficiently—preserving their fat-free muscle mass to a much greater extent and exhibiting fewer extreme drops in metabolic and endocrine hormone markers. 

Lead researcher James McClung noted that while both sexes suffered identical declines in sleep quality and physical output metrics over the two-month course, female physiology proved remarkably resilient against prolonged starvation and multi-stressor exhaustion, concluding: "An elite warfighter is an elite warfighter. March 4, 2002. A 10,000-foot freezing mountain peak in eastern Afghanistan: Takur Ghar.

When a Navy SEAL was thrown from a damaged Chinook into an enemy hornets' nest, Air Force Combat Controller John Chapman volunteered to go back onto that mountain to get his brother back.

As soon as their helicopter touched down, they were hit with RPGs and heavy machine-gun fire. Chapman charged uphill alone through thigh-deep snow, assaulted an al-Qaeda bunker, and neutralized the fighters inside.

While assaulting a second bunker, he was shot multiple times and knocked unconscious. Believed to be fallen, his team was forced to break contact down the mountain.

But John Chapman wasn’t dead.

Sixteen years later, declassified high-definition drone footage revealed the truth: Chapman woke up alone on that freezing peak. Severely wounded and surrounded by dozens of enemy fighters, he refused to quit.

For over an hour, he fought a solo one-man stand from a snow bunker.

When an inbound quick-reaction helicopter carrying 18 Army Rangers flew directly into the ambush zone, Chapman knew they would be shredded.

He made his final choice: he stepped out of his bunker into the open, drawing all enemy fire toward himself to protect the landing helicopter until he was mortally wounded.

His solo stand saved the lives of every man on that incoming bird.

In 2018, Master Sergeant John Chapman was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor—the first Air Force special operator to receive it since Vietnam.
